full_name: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
literary_identity: English peer and moralist whose Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times (1711) made politeness, wit and ridicule the tests of virtue and of religious sincerity.
biography: Born in London on 26 February 1671 and named for his grandfather, the First Earl of Shaftesbury, he was educated privately under the supervision of John Locke and kept only a brief residence at Oxford. He sat in the Commons for Christchurch from 1695 until he succeeded to the earldom in 1699. A failing chest ended any political career, and from 1704 he travelled for his health in the Netherlands and in Italy, corresponding with Dutch and French heterodox writers. He revised the essays, letters and dialogues of those years into Characteristics (1711), which he superintended through the press himself and introduced with a Design'd Letter satirising bookmaking. He died at Consendula in Calabria on 4 February 1713, leaving a daughter; the earldom passed to a nephew.
literary_profile: A philosopher of polite conversation who wrote in genres - letter, dialogue, soliloquy, rhapsody - and treated the inspection of one's own heart as a moral exercise.
stylistic_characteristics: Aphoristic, urbane and deliberately witty; sustained irony and theatrical self-examination; long periodic sentences pointed by sententious tags; argument conducted as banter.
intellectual_concerns: An innate moral sense and self-approval; enthusiasm, superstition and the ridicule of fanatics; the fitness of religion to common sense; politeness, reputation and the love of one's country.
historical_significance: He set the terms of eighteenth-century moral-sense theory and of the age's debate about enthusiasm, influencing Hutcheson, Hume, Adam Smith, Chesterfield, Voltaire and Kant, and making ridicule a standard weapon against priestcraft.
major_influences: Anthony Ashley Cooper, First Earl of Shaftesbury
biographical_uncertainty: Several pieces in Characteristics circulated in manuscript and in unauthorized copies, so the order of composition is still debated.

literary_identity: London physician and satirist whose Fable of the Bees (1714) argued that private vices, worked through vanity and emulation, produce public benefits.
biography: Born at Rotterdam about 1670 into a medical family, he trained in medicine in the Dutch Republic, spent time in France, and from the 1690s practised as a physician in London. His Grumbling Hive (1705) was reissued in 1714 as The Fable of the Bees: or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits, with prose remarks on the paradox. A medical treatise on the hypochondriacal and hysterick passions (1715) and Free Thoughts on Religion, the Church and National Happiness (1720) established him as a sceptical physician-philosopher. The enlarged Fable of 1723, with its Essay on Charity and Charity-Schools, was presented by the Middlesex grand jury as a public nuisance and denounced from pulpits. He added a second part in 1729 and an anonymous enquiry into the original of honour in 1732, which broke with the moral-sense creed of the late Earl of Shaftesbury. He died at Hackney on 21 January 1733.
literary_profile: A clinical satirist of commercial society who turned the maxim tradition of the French moralists into an unsentimental analysis of appetite, flattery and trade.
stylistic_characteristics: Tight Augustan couplets and deadpan prose paradox; fable, dialogue and case history; medical and commercial vocabulary; a sardonic refusal to moralise.
intellectual_concerns: Vice as the motor of prosperity; vanity, luxury and emulation; the hypocrisy of public benevolence; the origin of honour and shame; the self-deception of the virtuous.
historical_significance: The Fable became the century's most provocative thesis about commercial society, censured in its own day and recovered later by writers from Adam Smith to Keynes as a forerunner of the economics of unintended consequences.
major_influences: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury, as his antagonist
biographical_uncertainty: His birth is only fixed approximately, about 1670; his early training and the details of his practice are thinly documented, and the dating of some tracts varies.

literary_identity: Ulster-born freethinker, heterodox scholar and hard-line Whig pamphleteer, a founding figure of English deism after Christianity Not Mysterious (1696).
biography: Born in 1670 on the Inishowen peninsula, of a Gaelic family whose name was anglicised from O'Tolian, he studied at Glasgow, at Edinburgh, where he took his MA, and at Leiden, acquiring an extraordinary range of languages. Christianity Not Mysterious (1696), arguing that the gospel holds nothing properly above reason, was ordered burned by civil and ecclesiastical authority and made him the most attacked writer of his generation. He moved in London Whig and commonwealth circles, edited Milton's prose, defended Lucan against his classical detractors, and wrote on party management, the Hanoverian succession and the Bible as history: Nazarenus (1718) recovered apocryphal gospel fragments, and Tetradymus (1720) gathered four sceptical treatises. His political work carried him between Dublin, London and the Hague, where he cultivated Leibniz and Berkeley; he died at Putney on 11 March 1722.
literary_profile: A combative polymath of letters, party and scripture, who treated the history of religion as a history of power and of priestly imposture.
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, allusive and polemic; scholarly footnotes used as weapons; blunt deistical reasoning dressed in commonwealth rhetoric; a restless, digressive pamphlet energy.
intellectual_concerns: The reduction of mystery to evidence; tolerance and its clerical enemies; the political history of the biblical canon; pantheistic materialism and the eternity of matter; the management of parties and the secret history of states.
historical_significance: He fixed the agenda of deism and of the historical criticism of Scripture, gave the commonwealth Whigs a model of scholarship in the service of liberty, and provoked the century's long rearguard action of Christian apologetics.
major_influences: the Latin and Dutch republican tradition
biographical_uncertainty: His degrees, employments and embassies are imperfectly documented and rest partly on his own claims; several works appeared anonymously.

literary_identity: Barrister and freethinker whose Essay Concerning the Use of Reason (1707) and inquiry on human liberty (1717) made him the boldest English deist before Hume.
biography: Born at Heston in Middlesex in 1676, he was educated at Eton and at King's College, Cambridge, and was called to the bar. He became the close friend and literary executor of John Locke, lived on a property in Lincolnshire, divided his years between Heston and Pall Mall, and gathered a club of free inquirers. His Essay Concerning the Use of Reason (1707) and the Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion (1707) drew a barrage of replies from churchmen, and the published correspondence with the Bishop of Winchester on the evidences of Christianity ran through 1708 and 1709. A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Human Liberty (1717) denied the liberty of indifference, and The Scheme of Literal Prophecy Considered (1727) denied that Old Testament prophecy proved the gospel. He died in London on 13 December 1729, and a servant's tale that he defied the priests on his deathbed was long printed as a model of infidel constancy.
literary_profile: A lawyer's deism: courteous, relentlessly procedural argument that demands of revelation the same evidence it would require in court.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, dry and forensic; scholastic distinctions and long chains of consequence; courteous invective; a fondness for published correspondence and formal rejoinder.
intellectual_concerns: The boundaries of reason in religion; liberty, necessity and the will; the evidential value of miracle and prophecy; priestly authority and the rights of private judgement; tolerance as a civil necessity.
historical_significance: He moved deism from a defence of natural religion into a historical and philosophical critique of revelation, and defined the freethinking tradition that Bentley, Clarke and Butler were recruited to answer.
major_influences: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
the Dutch Cartesian and Spinozist milieu
biographical_uncertainty: The celebrated deathbed declaration is reported by a hostile servant and is generally doubted by modern scholars.

literary_identity: Civil lawyer and deist, author of Rights of the Christian Church (1706) and of Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), the creed-book of eighteenth-century deism.
biography: Born at Bere Ferrers in Devon, probably in 1657, the son of a clergyman, he went up to Oxford, where he sat at Lincoln and Exeter and became a fellow of All Souls. He conformed to Rome during the reign of James II and returned to the Church of England after the Revolution, an episode that sharpened his lifelong interest in church authority. The Rights of the Christian Church (1706) argued for a national establishment controlled by the state and answered his High Church critics; Vindiciae Judaeorum (1707) defended the Jewish nation against slanders. Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730), published anonymously as the work of a person of the Church of England, reduced the gospel to a republication of the religion of nature and provoked dozens of answers within a year. He died on 16 August 1733.
literary_profile: The systematiser of deism, who read Christianity as a moral institution whose truth must be measurable by a reason common to all nations.
stylistic_characteristics: Arid, lawyerly, definitional prose; axioms and corollaries and exhaustive division of terms; a polemical coolness that invites reply rather than assent.
intellectual_concerns: The reasonableness and universality of natural religion; the civil rights of churches and the reach of state supremacy; priestcraft, mystery and the commerce of God with man; the interests of Israel and of toleration.
historical_significance: Christianity as Old as the Creation gave deism its mature form and forced the apologetic literature of the 1730s into a defensive debate about reason, revelation and the political power of clergy.
major_influences: Edward Herbert, First Baron of Cherbury
the Erasmian and Socinian critique of priestcraft
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is only approximately fixed, and his principal works were issued anonymously, complicating attribution.

literary_identity: Nonjuring clergyman and devotional writer, author of A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1728) and of the Christian perfection tracts that shaped Methodist and Anglo-Catholic piety.
biography: Born at King's Cliffe in Northamptonshire in 1686, he was educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and held a fellowship there. He refused the oaths to the Hanoverian succession in 1715, lost his fellowship and spent the following decade as a schoolmaster in London. Retiring to his birthplace in 1727, he lived there, writing and governing his household, until his death in 1761. In 1726 he entered the stage controversy with an attack on theatrical entertainment as a snare of Satan; in 1728 A Serious Call applied the rules of devotion to the ordinary hours of a gentleman's or a lady's day. From the 1730s his letters on the spirit of prayer and on the spirit of faith set him against Bishop Warburton; with the help of the lawyer William Bryan he edited and translated Jacob Boehme and printed a selection of Boehme's works in 1745.
literary_profile: A practical diviner of the daily closet, whose prose makes the whole of life, and not its religious intervals, an offering.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, urgent, exact devotional prose; moral portraiture and example; a rule-of-life cadence of precept, reproof and prayer; later a mystical exuberance of type and figure.
intellectual_concerns: The universality of devotion; Christian perfection and the death of self-will; church, oath and civil obedience; the stage, dress and the amusements of the world; the hidden God of Boehmean mysticism.
historical_significance: The Serious Call made him the most read English devotional writer between Bunyan and the Tractarians; it formed the religious imagination of Samuel Johnson and of the Oxford movement, and his mystical writings fed Methodist and Anglo-Catholic holiness.
major_influences: the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer
biographical_uncertainty: His reasons for conforming outwardly after 1727 are debated, and the serial publication of his letters makes their chronology awkward.

literary_identity: Anglican bishop and the most formidable Christian apologist of the century, author of the Analogy of Religion (1736) and of the sermons on human nature.
biography: Born at Wantage in Berkshire in 1692 into a Presbyterian family, he was designed for the Dissent and educated under Dissenting tutors in London before turning to the Church of England and entering Oriel College, Oxford. His published correspondence with Samuel Clarke on the foundation of virtue and moral government (1716) gave him an early philosophical reputation, and he was chosen a fellow of his college. As preacher at the Rolls Chapel he delivered the sermons on human nature, conscience and self-love printed in 1726. The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed, to the Constitution and Course of Nature (1736), answering the deists of his day by arguing that the course of nature is as full of mystery and difficulty as revelation, made him the acknowledged champion of his church. Preferred by Queen Caroline, he was clerk of the closet, then bishop of Bristol, dean of St Paul's and, from 1750, bishop of Durham. He died at Bath on 16 June 1752.
literary_profile: A casuist of common sense who argued from probability, analogy and the structure of the mind rather than from demonstration.
stylistic_characteristics: Balanced, deliberate, heavily qualified prose; a preacher's plainness sharpened by philosopher's distinctions; patient enumeration of cases and the famous weight given to probability.
intellectual_concerns: Conscience as supreme authority within the mind; selfishness and benevolence; the analogies between nature and revelation; theodicy and future punishment; the historical evidences of Christianity.
historical_significance: His Analogy set the terms of British natural theology for a century, and his account of conscience and of the plurality of motives shaped British moral philosophy and theology alike.
major_influences: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology of his academy years and his Oxford degrees is imperfectly documented.

literary_identity: Irish-born philosopher and Church of Ireland bishop whose immaterialism, theory of vision and Alciphron make him one of the two or three metaphysicians whom the century could not ignore.
biography: Born at Thomastown in County Kilkenny in 1685, he went to Trinity College Dublin, where he became a fellow and a tutor, and in 1707 took his degree. In a single brilliant period of young manhood he published the Essay towards a New Theory of Vision (1709), the Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) and the Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous (1713), which reduced sensible qualities to ideas in a mind and made the existence of matter depend on being perceived. Ordained in the Church of Ireland and appointed dean of Derry in 1724, he married Esther Vanhomrigh in 1723 and spent a decade in America trying to fund a college in Bermuda. The failure of that scheme ended his hopes of a transatlantic church; from 1734 he lived as bishop of Cloyne, where he wrote Siris (1744) on tar-water as a remedy, and he died at Oxford on 14 January 1753.
literary_profile: A philosopher of perception and language who argued that mind, not matter, is the ground of the visible world, and who wrote his hardest metaphysics as lively dialogue.
stylistic_characteristics: Sparse, precise, almost aphoristic argument; numbered propositions and sharp objection-and-reply; a sceptic's ingenuity in the service of a pastor's conclusions.
intellectual_concerns: The nature of ideas, perception and the external world; abstraction and the misuse of signs in language; the absolute space and time of the Newtonians; the reality of spirit and active agency; religious language and the minute philosopher.
historical_significance: He carried early modern empiricism to its sceptical limit, anticipated later work on vision and on language, and supplied Hume, Reid and the whole tradition of idealism with the problems they inherited.
major_influences: the new mathematics and Newtonian natural philosophy
biographical_uncertainty: The details of the Bermuda college scheme and of his American years survive unevenly, and his motives for the enterprise are still argued.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Anglo-Irish moral philosopher of the Scottish Presbyterian tradition
literary_identity: Seceding minister and first professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow, who founded the moral-sense school and taught the generation that carried natural rights into the Atlantic revolutions.
biography: Born at Saintfield in County Down in 1694 into a Scottish Presbyterian family, he studied at Glasgow and was licensed by the Associate or Seceding ministry, though he soon gave up preaching for teaching. He kept a school in Dublin, and in 1730 was appointed to the newly founded chair of moral philosophy at Glasgow, which he held until his death. His Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue (1725), with its defence of a disinterested moral sense against Mandeville, and his Essay on the Passions (1728) established a new science of approval. His System of Moral Philosophy was published after his death in 1755 from his manuscripts and lectures. He died in Dublin on 8 August 1746.
literary_profile: The systematizer of sentiment as a moral faculty, who located virtue in benevolence toward the greatest number rather than in self-interest or in reason alone.
stylistic_characteristics: Textbook plainness with a preacher's warmth; definitions, divisions and a running argument with opponents; a vocabulary of sense, taste, benevolence and approval.
intellectual_concerns: Moral sense and disinterested benevolence; the happiness of the greatest number; the distinction of natural and moral good; the right of resistance and limited government; the senses and the relish of beauty.
historical_significance: He founded the sentimental and utilitarian strands of eighteenth-century ethics, taught the generation that framed American natural-rights politics, and made benevolence a central term of moral philosophy.
major_influences: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
biographical_uncertainty: The dating of his Dublin academy years is uncertain; his Irish and Ulster origins are documented but his university career was cut short by his early death.

literary_identity: Philosopher, essayist and historian of the Scottish Enlightenment, the most rigorous sceptic in English prose, whose Treatise and Enquiries remade the theory of knowledge, morals and politics.
biography: Born in Edinburgh in April 1711 into a small landowning family, he was educated at home and at the university, tried a merchant's life in Bristol, and then withdrew to France to write. The Treatise of Human Nature (1739-40) appeared to little acclaim, and he confessed his distress at its neglect; the moral and political essays of 1741 and the Enquiries of 1748 and 1751 restated the same philosophy in a public style. He was blocked from an Edinburgh professorship in 1745 by clerical opposition and was summoned before the presbytery of that city in 1756 without being censured; he earned his living as a private tutor, as keeper of the Advocates' Library and, from 1754, as a historian, and his History of England made him wealthy. He served in the embassy in Paris from 1763, briefly at the foreign office, and accompanied Rousseau to England in 1766 before their quarrel. He died in Edinburgh on 25 August 1776, having written his own short account of a life he called so little interrupted.
literary_profile: A sceptical humanist who reduced causation, induction, the self and moral obligation to habit, sentiment and custom, yet wrote with an urbanity that made disbelief amiable.
stylistic_characteristics: Lucid, measured, ironized prose; the clean paragraph of the Enquiries; examples drawn from common life; dry humour and a refusal of technical jargon; historical narrative of stately balance.
intellectual_concerns: Custom as the guide of life; the limits of reason in belief and in morals; the passions and the rules of justice; natural religion, miracle and the design argument; the principles of taste, party and commerce.
historical_significance: He set the agenda of post-Kantian philosophy in the problem of induction and personal identity, founded the empirical study of religion and of politics, and gave classical liberalism its sceptical defence of convention.
major_influences: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
Cicero and the moralists of the Roman Republic
biographical_uncertainty: The details of his father's estate, his Bristol period and his Parisian secretarial work are patchy; his posthumous Dialogues were published in 1779 under his brother's editorship against his own instructions on timing.

literary_identity: Moral philosopher and political economist of Glasgow and Kirkcaldy, author of The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776).
biography: Born at Kirkcaldy in 1723 and educated at Glasgow and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he found the place intellectually barren, he returned to Scotland and began public lectures in Edinburgh in 1748 with the encouragement of Lord Kames. He was appointed successively to the chairs of logic and of moral philosophy at Glasgow, where his teaching on jurisprudence, rhetoric and police shaped a generation. The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), built on sympathy and the impartial spectator, made his reputation. As tutor to the young Duke of Buccleuch he spent nearly two years in France, meeting philosophes and physiocrats, and then retired to Kirkcaldy to write, publishing the Wealth of Nations in 1776 with Strahan and Cadell. He took office as a commissioner of customs in Edinburgh in 1778, became a fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh and was elected lord rector of Glasgow. He died in Edinburgh on 17 July 1790, having asked that his unpublished manuscripts be destroyed; the Essays on Philosophical Subjects, a posthumous volume, appeared in 1795.
literary_profile: A moral philosopher of commercial society who joined the analysis of sympathy to the analysis of exchange, and wrote economic reasoning as part of ethics.
stylistic_characteristics: Long, periodic, expository prose built from illustration and qualification; a lecturer's plainness and abundance of example; irony directed at merchants, ministers and monopolists.
intellectual_concerns: Sympathy, propriety and the impartial spectator; the division of labour, self-interest and the invisible hand of adjustment; the history of civil society and the effects of commerce; justice, utility and the proper limits of government.
historical_significance: He founded political economy as a systematic discipline and remains the reference point of liberal arguments about markets, while his moral philosophy has been recovered as the indispensable half of his work.
major_influences: the Scottish jurists of natural law
biographical_uncertainty: His lecture notes survive only in student reports and later copies, so the chronology and content of his teaching on jurisprudence are disputed.

literary_identity: Minister and professor of Glasgow, founder of the school of common-sense philosophy, who answered the ideal theory of Locke, Berkeley and Hume by appealing to the first principles of human understanding.
biography: Born in the manse at Strachan in the Mearns in 1710, the son of a Church of Scotland minister, he studied at King's College, Aberdeen, was licensed as a preacher in his teens and served the parish of New Machar from 1737. He left the ministry for teaching in 1752, when he was appointed regent in moral philosophy at King's College, Old Aberdeen, where the lectures sharpened his case against the ideal theory. His Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764) argued that perception, memory and belief are original faculties that need no deduction, and that the way of ideas ends in Humean doubt. His Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764) argued that perception, memory and belief are original faculties that require no deduction, and that the way of ideas ends in Humean doubt. Called in 1764 to the Glasgow chair of moral philosophy after Smith's resignation, he held it until failing health forced his retirement in 1781, publishing the Essays on the Intellectual Powers (1785) and the Essays on the Active Powers (1788). He died in Glasgow on 7 October 1796.
literary_profile: A pastor-philosopher who treated scepticism as a disease of theory and met it with an inventory of the mind's innate testimonies.
stylistic_characteristics: Patient, encyclopaedic and repetitive exposition; classification of faculties and first principles; concrete appeals to sight, testimony and the language of common life, in a minister's measured tones.
intellectual_concerns: Perception, suggestion and the belief in external existence; the principles that precede reasoning; testimony, language and the rights of common sense; moral obligation, conscience and liberty of agency.
historical_significance: He gave philosophy its common-sense tradition, shaped the Scottish and American schools of mind, and set the problem of how to answer idealist scepticism that later thinkers from the Scottish realists to the twentieth century inherited.
major_influences: the Aberdeen faculty psychology of his teachers
biographical_uncertainty: His published output is slight compared with his lectures, and the ordering of his intellectual development before 1764 must be reconstructed from manuscripts.

literary_identity: Minister, army chaplain and professor at Edinburgh, whose Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767) made commercial progress and the loss of civic spirit a single problem.
biography: Born at Leith in 1723, the son of the town's minister, he was educated at Edinburgh, was licensed as a preacher and served as a regimental chaplain abroad during the Seven Years' War. In 1764 he supplied the Glasgow lectures left uncovered when Adam Smith went abroad with the Duke of Buccleuch, and in the same year was appointed to the Edinburgh chair of moral philosophy, which he held until his resignation. His Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767) and the four-volume History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic (1769) won him a wide reading in Britain and France, and he helped found the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1783. His Principles of Moral and Political Science, from his lectures, appeared in 1792 and his Institutes of Moral Science posthumously in 1823. He was a friend of Hume, Smith, Robertson and Carlyle, and a frequent visitor to Paris and Geneva. He died in 1816.
literary_profile: The moral historian of civil society, who read history as the unintended product of human action and warned that commerce could purchase comfort at the cost of citizenship.
stylistic_characteristics: Large-swinging historical prose, sententious and rhetorical; generalisation from ancient and modern instances; a preacher's cadence and a stadial theorist's confidence in periods and stages.
intellectual_concerns: Stages of society from savage to commercial life; the unintended consequences of action; corruption, arms and civic participation; the psychological costs of the division of labour; the Roman republic as a mirror of modern politics.
historical_significance: His Essay founded the sociological reading of history and supplied the republican critique of commercial modernity that later political theory, from Marx to Arendt, has reused.
biographical_uncertainty: The dating of his lecture courses and the relationship between his published works and his teaching manuscripts remain matters of scholarly argument.

literary_identity: Regius Professor of Civil Law at Glasgow, who turned the history of ranks and of property into an explanation of law, government and the condition of women.
biography: Born at the manse of Kirk o'Shotts in 1735, the son of the parish minister, he was educated at Glasgow, where he sat under Adam Smith, and became an advocate. With the support of Adam Smith and of the Duke of Buccleuch he was appointed in 1761 to the Glasgow chair of civil law, which he held until his death. His Origin of the Distinction of Ranks (1771) explained subordination as the consequence of subsistence, marriage and property rather than of nature, and drew a friendly critique of its chapter on women from John Dalton, printed with later editions. His Historical View of the English Government from the Settlement of the Saxons to the Revolution of 1688 (1787) applied the same method to English liberty and to the growth of the commercial orders. A sympathiser with the French Revolution after 1789, he was harassed by the alarm of the 1790s. He died on 30 May 1801.
literary_profile: The most systematic of the Scottish historians of society, who wrote the equality of conditions as a question of law, labour and domestic authority.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, cumulative, lecture-hall prose; long historical sequences argued from causes; a lawyer's precision about ranks, tenures and rights; comparatively little ornament.
intellectual_concerns: The dependence of political authority on property; the origins of rank, servitude and gender subordination; the history of law as social history; the foundations of English liberty and of representative government.
historical_significance: He carried stadial conjectural history into the analysis of class and of the family, and became a chief source for later theories of social development, including the tradition that linked property to political power.
biographical_uncertainty: His published works are only parts of a large lecture output, some of which survives in student notes of uncertain date.

literary_identity: Aberdeen professor and poet, the most widely read assailant of Humean scepticism, whose Essay on Truth (1770) and The Minstrel (1771) made him a European name.
biography: Born at Laurencekirk in 1735, the son of a shopkeeper and small farmer, he was educated at Marischal College, Aberdeen, took his MA in 1753 and served briefly as a schoolmaster. He was appointed in 1760 to the Marischal chair of moral philosophy and logic, which he held for four decades, and married Mary Dun in 1767. The Essay on Truth (1770), a robust defence of common sense against the ideal system, made his reputation and earned him a pension from George III; the didactic poem The Minstrel, with its sketch of a young genius, followed in 1771 and was enlarged in 1773. His essays on poetry and music were gathered with the rest of his later writing in the Dissertations Moral and Critical of 1796, after the period covered here. He corresponded with Johnson and Witherspoon and was widely praised, and for a generation his name stood in the American colleges for the Christian answer to scepticism. He died in Aberdeen on 16 February 1803.
literary_profile: A professor of common sense and of taste, who argued that scepticism refutes itself in the ordinary belief of mankind and versified the same appeal to feeling.
stylistic_characteristics: Confident, declamatory argument and good-humoured invective; descriptive and personifying verse in a meditative, Thomson-like manner; a didactic plainness of diction.
intellectual_concerns: The instincts and the first principles of knowledge; the reality of the external world and of other minds; genius, taste and the psychology of poetry; the moral sentiments and their cultural conditions.
historical_significance: For a generation he was the standard answer to Hume in Britain and above all in the American colleges, and his career shows both the strength and the superficiality of the common-sense assault on scepticism.
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology of his abolitionist writing and the extent of his debt to Reid's unpublished teaching are still debated.

literary_identity: Judge of the Court of Session and polymath of Edinburgh, the patron and publisher of the Scottish Enlightenment, whose Sketches of the History of Man tried to write the whole of society as natural history.
biography: Born about 1696 at Kames House in Berwickshire and educated largely at home, he became an advocate and built a leading practice at the Scottish bar. He rose to the bench of the Court of Session in 1752 as Lord Kames and sat there until his death, taking a prominent part in the political and cultural life of Edinburgh. His Historical Law-Tracts (1732) read early law as evidence of early society; his Essays on the Principles of Morality and Natural Religion (1751), which grounded morals in instinct rather than in revelation, were censured by the church courts. Elements of Criticism (1762) analysed the passions and the effects of the beautiful and the sublime, and the four-volume Sketches of the History of Man (1774) surveyed races, languages, government and agriculture as a single natural history. He encouraged and published the younger writers around him, and died in Edinburgh on 27 December 1782.
literary_profile: A lawyer-naturalist of society who treated customs, laws and tastes as specimens to be classified rather than as doctrines to be defended.
stylistic_characteristics: Miscellaneous, encyclopaedic and aphoristic; numbered propositions, cases and historical instances; a judge's love of definition combined with an amateur's appetite for generalisation.
intellectual_concerns: The historical development of law and property; the instincts underlying morality and religion; the physiology of the passions and the analysis of aesthetic effect; the comparative history of races and of the stages of society.
historical_significance: He gave the Scottish Enlightenment its institutional encouragement and its model of conjectural history, and his criticism of the passions shaped the aesthetic theory of his century.
biographical_uncertainty: The year of his birth is only approximately fixed, and his authorship of some tracts and his role in the patronage of others are difficult to separate.

literary_identity: Physician and Dissenting philosopher whose Observations on Man (1749) built a complete system of mind, morals and religion on the doctrine of association of ideas.
biography: Baptised at Luddenden near Halifax in 1705, the son of a poor clergyman, he lost both parents early and was brought up by an uncle. Educated at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he took his degrees and later his MD, he abandoned a clerical career, studied medicine in London and at Cambridge and practised successively in the provinces, in London and at Bath. His early medical studies prepared his larger scheme, which reduced mental life to vibration, sensation and the association of ideas as Locke had described them. Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Anticipations (1749, two volumes) derived the whole of ethics, religion and hope from that mechanism, and its second part argued for a future state of universal happiness. He married and had several children, and died at Bath in 1757.
literary_profile: The architect of associationist psychology, who made the mechanical linking of ideas the explanation of character, virtue and religious expectation.
stylistic_characteristics: Tight, numbered, propositional prose; long chains of deduction from a single principle; a physician's plainness and a dissenting divinity's earnestness of reference.
intellectual_concerns: Association as the law of mind; the physiological basis of thought; the derivation of moral sense from education and habit; the accumulation of desires and the scheme of future happiness; necessitation and prayer.
historical_significance: His Observations founded the associationist tradition that Priestley, Darwin, the Mills and the psychology of the next century developed, and made the link between mind and mechanism a standard explanatory programme.
biographical_uncertainty: The date and exact place of his birth are uncertain; his son's memoir and later accounts disagree on the details.

literary_identity: Oxford don, serjeant at law, judge and Tory MP, whose four-volume Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765-1769) made English law a readable rational system.
biography: Born in Cheapside in London in 1723, the posthumous son of a City merchant, he was educated at a London grammar school and at Pembroke College, Oxford, with the help of relations, and was elected a fellow of All Souls. Called to the bench of the Middle Temple and practising on the Oxford and home circuits, he won fame by a book on gavelkind and by lecturing on English law, which led to his appointment as the first Vinerian professor in 1758. His Analysis of the Laws of England (1756) and his Discourse on the Study of the Law (1765) prepared the Commentaries, published in four parts between 1765 and 1769 and immediately made his name. He sat in the Commons, was appointed to the bench of the Common Pleas and knighted in 1770, and was transferred to the King's Bench in 1779, where his rigorous, sometimes unpopular judgments tested his own theory of law. He died in London on 14 February 1780.
literary_profile: The great systematiser and apologist of the common law, who presented its intricacies as an ordered, decent and largely admirable inheritance.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, stately, judicious prose that explains difficulty without hiding it; balanced periods and a scholar's courtesy; historical narrative used to legitimate existing doctrine.
intellectual_concerns: The reasonableness and continuity of the common law; the rights of persons and of things; the nature of law, sovereignty and the reach of parliamentary authority; the legal condition of servants, women, children and colonial subjects; the relation of law to religion and morality.
historical_significance: The Commentaries became the standard education of English-speaking lawyers for two centuries and, with their American reprints, one of the chief sources of early American legal and political vocabulary; Bentham's attack on them opened the age of law reform.
major_influences: the civilians and canonists of Oxford
biographical_uncertainty: The order and dating of his lectures and of the several editions of the Commentaries, which he revised to his death, are complex and disputed.

literary_identity: Historian of the decline and fall of the Roman Empire, whose six volumes (1776-1788) made the fate of ancient civilisation and of Christianity the central narrative of the age.
biography: Born at Putney in 1737, a delicate child largely left to his own reading, he went up to Oxford in 1752, was converted to Rome there and was removed from the university, and spent several formative years at Lausanne under a Calvinist pastor. He returned to Protestantism, read widely in French and Latin, and served in the Hampshire militia during the Seven Years' War without seeing action. In 1764 he reached Rome, and among the ruins of the Capitoline resolved to write the history of its decline. The first volume of the Decline and Fall appeared in 1776, the second and third in 1781 and the last three in 1788; between them he sat in Parliament, took office at the board of trade, and endured a hostile controversy over his fifteenth and sixteenth chapters, which he answered in 1779. He fell with the North ministry in 1782, settled for years at Lausanne with his friend Deyverdun, and completed his history there before returning to London, where he died in January 1794.
literary_profile: A philosophic historian who explained empires by manners, superstition and circumstance, and whose irony gave religious narrative the poise of an autumn evening.
stylistic_characteristics: A grand periodic style of balanced clauses and weighted antithesis; sustained irony that never declares itself; narrative panache in collapse and battle; a footnotes apparatus of learning used as concealed argument.
intellectual_concerns: The causes of the fall of the western empire; the relation of Christianity to the decline of civic and military virtue; superstition, enthusiasm and ecclesiastical history; national character, barbarism and the progress of society.
historical_significance: The Decline and Fall set the modern standard of source-based secular history and remains the model of historical narrative in English; its account of the triumph of the church has been argued over ever since.
major_influences: the French philosophes of the Encyclopedie
biographical_uncertainty: The exact circumstances of his Oxford expulsion and conversion, and the dates of several of his own memoirs, remain imperfectly settled.

literary_identity: Minister of the Church of Scotland, principal of Edinburgh and royal historiographer, whose History of America (1777) made philosophical history a professional discipline in Britain.
biography: Born at Borthwick near Langholm in 1721, the son of a country clergyman, he was educated at Edinburgh, entered the ministry and served a southern parish before he removed to Edinburgh and became one of the city's most fashionable preachers. The History of Scotland (1759) established him as the leading historian of his generation, and the great work on the reign of Charles V (1769) displayed his command of archives and of the European sixteenth century. Appointed principal of the University of Edinburgh in 1762 and royal historiographer, he at last produced the History of America (1777), three volumes of sources, geography, conquest and character which were translated across Europe, and the History of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth (1787). His disquisition on the ancients' knowledge of India came in 1791, after the period with which this record deals. He was a leader of the moderate interest in the church, a friend of Hume, Smith, Ferguson and Home, and died in 1793.
literary_profile: The historian of states and religions who wrote narrative as instructed enquiry, combining Scottish church politics with the sources of the Spanish and Italian archives.
stylistic_characteristics: Dignified, lucid, well-paced narrative; disquisitions and notes carrying the argument; a preacher's moral seriousness and an editor's restraint; balance of character, cause and consequence.
intellectual_concerns: The origins of American civilisation and conquest; the political and religious history of Europe in the age of Charles V; feudal law, ranks and the rise of the commons; the character of Queen Elizabeth and of the Reformation.
historical_significance: He professionalised historical writing in Britain, gave the English-speaking world its standard account of America's discovery and conquest, and set the model of philosophic narrative that Gibbon and the nineteenth century inherited.
major_influences: the Spanish and Italian historians whose sources he used
biographical_uncertainty: His early parish years are documented thinly, and his use of other men's manuscripts and collections has been re-assessed by later scholarship.

literary_identity: Unitarian minister, chemist and controversialist who isolated the gas he called dephlogisticated air and who argued that the same free enquiry applied to matter, to government and to Christian doctrine.
biography: Born at Birstfield in Yorkshire in 1733, the son of a clothier and a dissenting mother, he was intended for the ministry, studied under Dissenting tutors, learned several languages and began to preach. He held small charges in Suffolk, taught for years at the academy in Warrington, and in the early 1760s began the electrical and chemical experiments that won him election to the Royal Society in 1766. Abandoning the doctrine of the Trinity, he served at Mill Hill in Leeds, acted as librarian and companion to the Earl of Shelburne on a continental tour, and settled in Birmingham in 1780 as minister of New Meeting, in the company of the natural philosophers and manufacturers of the Lunar Society circle. His Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air (1774-1777) made him famous; his Institutes of Natural and Revealed Religion, his Essay on a Doctrine of Scriptural Necessity and his histories of early Christian opinion attacked corruptions he believed priests had introduced. His defence of the French Revolution, printed in 1791, brought a mob to Birmingham, and he emigrated to Pennsylvania, where he died in 1804.
literary_profile: An investigator who refused the distinction between laboratory and pulpit, and whose prose kept the plain, earnest manner of the practical dissenting preacher.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, unadorned, accumulative expository prose; experiment described in reproducible detail; polemic conducted as historical evidence and close reading of texts; a controversialist's appetite for reply.
intellectual_concerns: The chemistry of the air and the phlogiston question; electricity, optics and the materialism of mind; the historical corruptions of Christianity and the rejection of the Trinity; political liberty, toleration and the progress of society.
historical_significance: He was a central figure of the Enlightenment's unite of science with radical religion and politics, a founder of modern gas chemistry, and the most feared Unitarian apologist of his day.
major_influences: the English and Dutch Socinian tradition
biographical_uncertainty: Priority in the discovery of oxygen, and the chronology of his religious conversion, are still argued between his partisans and historians of chemistry.

literary_identity: Unitarian minister at Newington Green and one of the century's most influential moral philosophers, whose sermons on liberty made him a European authority on the rights of man.
biography: Born at Bristol in 1723 and apprenticed to a glover, he found his vocation in the Dissent, studied mathematics, philosophy and a range of languages, and in the late 1750s became the minister of a small congregation at Newington Green, where he lived for the rest of his life. His Review of the Principal Questions in Morals (1769), a rigorous attack on sentiment and self-love as the foundation of right, gave him a philosophical rank beside Butler and Reid. Mathematical and demographic papers on annuities, life assurance and the value of marriage and mortality tables made him a Fellow of the Royal Society and an adviser to government on the funding of life. His sermons and tracts on the American Revolution, on the love of one's country, on toleration and on the corruptions of civil and ecclesiastical liberty were read, reviewed and answered across Britain, France and America. He died at Newington Green in June 1791, having refused richer preferment and stayed with his small meeting.
literary_profile: A moralist of reason and rights, who held that right and wrong are as fixed as the relations of number and that government exists only by the trust of the governed.
stylistic_characteristics: Austere, tightly argued plainness; definitions and divisions carried into pulpit oratory; arithmetic and actuarial precision applied to human affairs; a sermonist's solemnity of appeal.
intellectual_concerns: Objective moral obligation against sentiment and interest; the reasonableness and corruptions of Christianity; the rights of individuals and the accountability of rulers; the valuation of life, annuities and population; the sin of the slave trade.
historical_significance: He supplied the rationalist morality and the doctrine of popular consent that made dissenting England a school of radical politics, and his actuarial work founded the mathematics of life assurance.
biographical_uncertainty: The dating of his early conversion to Unitarian beliefs is loose, and the full text of several sermons survives only in reports made from shorthand.

literary_identity: Artisan, excise officer and the most powerful political pamphleteer of the Atlantic revolutions, whose Common Sense (1776) turned revolt into ordinary language.
biography: Born at Thetford in 1737, the son of a Quaker staymaker, he served his father's trade, ran briefly and failed at several ventures, and became an officer of excise, a posting he lost after he had petitioned Parliament on his colleagues' pay. Frustrated and in debt, he went to London, fell in with Benjamin Franklin and reached Philadelphia at the end of 1774 with letters of introduction. He began to write for the Pennsylvania Magazine, where in March 1775 appeared his first and sharpest attack on American slavery, and in January 1776 Common Sense, arguing for independence and a republic in prose the mechanic could read. The American Crisis papers, written through the war, were read to Washington's troops; he served the American cause as a writer and in public office, and after the war was rewarded by several states. He returned to England in 1787, and his Rights of Man (1791) and the first part of The Age of Reason (1794), both after the period covered here, made him a prosecuted and then an exiled figure; he died in New York in 1809.
literary_profile: The democrat of plain style, who treated government as a common trade, monarchy as an imposture, and the reader's good sense as the only authority worth obeying.
stylistic_characteristics: Short declarative sentences, homely metaphor and moral indignation; argument as address, with the cadence of a sermon and the directness of a handbill; sarcasm directed at rank and priestcraft.
intellectual_concerns: Natural rights and the consent of the governed; the corruption of hereditary and ministerial power; the sin and economics of slavery; deistical religion against priestly and scriptural authority; the interests of labouring men.
historical_significance: He made the case for American independence to the people who had to fight for it, and his later radicalism set the template for popular republicanism, free-thought agitation and the nineteenth-century radical press.
major_influences: the English Dissenting and freethinking pamphlet tradition
biographical_uncertainty: His early manhood is dimly documented, and some of the works attributed to him in the 1770s have been disputed.

literary_identity: Law reformer and moral philosopher, founder of classical utilitarianism, who measured institutions by pleasure and pain and subjected the common law, the church and the prison to the test of utility.
biography: Born in London in 1748 into a wealthy family of attorneys, a child prodigy in Latin and French law books, he was educated at Queen's College, Oxford, and was called to the bar in 1769, though he never practised and soon abandoned the profession to write on legislation. He inherited property and leisure, attached himself to no party, and passed his life in lodgings and in correspondence, drafting codes, inspecting prisons, and corresponding with rulers and reformers across Europe and America. Two long stays at the estates of his brother Samuel, the engineer in Russia, sharpened his ideas about inspection and the organisation of labour. He wrote against Blackstone in the 1760s, published the Fragment on Government anonymously in 1776, the Defence of Usury in 1787 and the Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation in 1789. His Panopticon scheme and his writings on colonies and on judicial procedure belong to the 1790s; the coded works edited for him by Dumont appeared in the 1800s, and his attack on Blackstone's Commentaries remained in manuscript until the twentieth century. He died in London in 1832, having asked that his body be dissected and preserved as his auto-icon.
literary_profile: A jurist of facts and consequences, whose vocabulary of utility, felicity and the greatest number recast moral and legal argument as an arithmetic of interests.
stylistic_characteristics: Technical, taxonomic, tireless prose; long definitions, enumerated situations and coined terms; polemic conducted through analysis rather than rhetoric; a satirist's dryness about lawyers and priests.
intellectual_concerns: The greatest happiness principle; the anatomy of law, sovereignty and obligation; punishment, deterrence and the inspection of the idle; the interests of women, of colonial subjects and of animals; the corruption of church, university and common law.
historical_significance: He founded utilitarian ethics and systematic law reform, shaped Victorian policing, education and welfare legislation, and made the critical test of institutions their consequences for the greatest number.
biographical_uncertainty: The order of his vast unpublished manuscripts, much of it first printed by editors after his death, makes the dating of his ideas a continual problem.

literary_identity: Archdeacon of Carlisle and the century's master of utilitarian divinity, whose Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) made happiness and obedience the whole of duty.
biography: Born at Peterborough in July 1743, the son of a clergyman who later became headmaster of the free school at Giggleswick, he was educated at that school and at Christ's College, Cambridge, where an idle first year was retrieved by hard reading, a fellowship and a tutorship that made him the most successful coach of his university. He took orders in the Church of England, held a succession of northern livings at Musgrave, Dalston and Appleby, and was made archdeacon of Carlisle in 1782. His Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) soon became a standard university text and the target of reviewers who thought it reduced virtue to expedience. His argument for the undesigned coincidence of the apostolic letters appeared in the Horae Paulinae of 1790, and his Evidences of Christianity (1794) and Natural Theology (1802), both later than the period covered here, long stood as textbooks in the schools of theology. He was installed at Bishopwearmouth in his last years and died on 25 May 1805.
literary_profile: A clear-eyed churchman who wrote the morality of obedience and the evidences of belief for a reading public that wanted argument in plain terms.
stylistic_characteristics: Conversational, concrete and unornamented; cases and common-life examples carried through a single rule; the plainness of a good tutor, with a polemicist's patience in reply.
intellectual_concerns: Utility as the measure of duty; the obligations imposed by civil government and by the established church; the evidences of revelation and the credibility of miracle; design in nature and the relation of pleasure to virtue.
historical_significance: He gave utilitarian ethics its first systematic ecclesiastical form and supplied the teleological argument in the version Mill and Darwin had to answer; his textbooks governed English theological education for a generation.
major_influences: the Cambridge divines of the established church
biographical_uncertainty: The order in which his preferments and lecture texts were produced is complicated by posthumous edition and by his own revisions.

literary_identity: Anglican priest, evangelist and organiser of the Methodists, whose sermons, journals, hymnals and rules of society made a religious revival into a permanent connection.
biography: Born at Epworth in 1703, the fifteenth of the children of Samuel Wesley, a country rector, and of Susanna Wesley, who governed the household and its education, he was sent to the Charterhouse and then to Christ Church, Oxford, where he was elected a fellow and took his degrees. Ordained in the Church of England, he went with his brother Charles to Georgia as a missionary in the mid-1730s and came home a failure in his own judgement. At a meeting in Aldersgate Street in May 1738 he described the assurance of his pardon, and in the following year he began to preach out of doors in Bristol at Whitefield's example, since the churches would not open to him. For fifty years he travelled through Britain and Ireland on horseback, organising societies, classes and bands, training lay preachers and holding annual conferences, and he wrote and printed for the movement with tireless industry: sermons on several occasions, Notes upon the New Testament, a Journal, a Christian Library and the Collection of Hymns of 1780. He defended the salvation of slaves in Thoughts upon Slavery (1775) and in his last years encouraged the parliamentary agitation against the trade. He died in London in March 1791, having preached almost to the end, and was buried beside his chapel in City Road.
literary_profile: A preacher-writer of enormous practical energy, whose plain prose and vigorous verse carried a revived religion to colliers, miners and farm servants.
stylistic_characteristics: Direct, urgent, colloquial sermon prose; rules, minutes and class lists shaped for use; a journal kept for the public; hymn and paraphrase verse of muscular, repetitive simplicity.
intellectual_concerns: Original sin and universal redemption; justification by faith and the witness of the Spirit; Christian perfection and the means of grace; free grace against Calvinist decree; Methodist discipline, education and the duty of saving souls.
historical_significance: He made Methodism, the largest religious movement of the century in the English-speaking world, and shaped the hymnody, revival practice and later social history of Britain and America.
major_influences: the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer
biographical_uncertainty: The tallies of his sermons and mileage are traditional estimates rather than records, and the editing of his Journal for publication was a work of self-presentation.

literary_identity: Anglican clergyman and the finest hymn-writer of the English revival, whose lyrics gave Methodism its voice and much of its theology.
biography: Born at Epworth in 1707, one of the numerous children of Samuel and Susanna Wesley, he was sent on a scholarship to Westminster School and from there to Christ Church, Oxford, where he kept a journal of his religious progress and joined with his brother John and a few friends in the small society later mocked as methodists. Ordained and briefly in Georgia with John, he returned to an assured conversion recorded in his journal in 1738, and thereafter preached as an assistant revival preacher while labouring chiefly in verse. He married Sarah Gwynne in 1749, lived for years near the Methodist work at Bristol, where the Wesleyan school at Kingswood was founded, and settled in London later, remaining an Anglican priest who disliked several of his brother's concessions. His collections of hymns, published singly and with John, begin with Hymns and Sacred Poems of 1739 and run through the following decades. He died in London in March 1788.
literary_profile: The lyric theologian of the revival, who put doctrine, penitence and joy into metres that congregations could carry away.
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, tuneful, ecstatic lyrics in common and ballad measures; first-person plural address; paradox, tenderness and bodily feeling; a gift for the repeating clause that binds a singing congregation.
intellectual_concerns: Assurance, atonement and the witness of the Spirit; the praise of God by redeemed creatures; the holy year of nativity, passion and resurrection; the communion of the faithful and the terrors of judgement.
historical_significance: He is the century's most sung religious poet in English and the founder of Methodist hymnody; his texts still stand in most English-speaking hymnals and shaped the devotional language of revival Christianity.
biographical_uncertainty: The number of hymns credited to him varies widely between early accounts and modern scholarship, and some of his texts were revised by others in transmission.

literary_identity: Calvinistic Methodist preacher of the Great Awakening, the first true celebrity of the Atlantic religious world, whose open-air sermons and journals moved crowds on two continents.
biography: Born at Gloucester in 1714, the son of an innkeeper who died while he was a child, he worked as a servant at the town grammar school and went up to Oxford in 1735 as a humble self-paying student, where he joined the small religious society and experienced the conversion he never ceased to describe. Ordained in the Church of England, he began to preach in the fields about Bristol in 1739 and in London's Moorfields, since the pulpits were closed to him, and crossed the Atlantic repeatedly, preaching through the colonies in 1739-40 and again on great touring circuits. His Calvinism separated him from John Wesley in the early 1740s, and he devoted much of his later energy to fundraising for the Georgia orphan house he called Bethesda and for the preaching houses his converts built. His journals and his Narrative of God's Dealings with Him (1740) made his inner life public property, and Benjamin Franklin, who printed them, left the most admired contemporary account of his command of crowds. He died at Newburyport in Massachusetts in September 1770 and was buried there beneath the pulpit he had used.
literary_profile: A declaimer of irresistible voice and posture who turned conversion narrative and printed publicity into an engine of revival.
stylistic_characteristics: Vocal, theatrical, extempore sermon style preserved imperfectly in print; vivid personal narrative; plain scriptural address with an actor's gesture; prolific printed circulars and journals.
intellectual_concerns: Election, new birth and the immediate call of the Spirit; the ministry of the word out of doors; the unity of the revival across the denominations; the religious education and charity of converts, and the problem of slavery in the colonies he loved.
historical_significance: He created the model of the transatlantic evangelist and gave the Great Awakening its public form, influencing American preaching, revivalism and the culture of religious celebrity.
major_influences: the Church of England catechetical tradition
the Dutch and English Calvinist preaching tradition
biographical_uncertainty: His early years at Oxford and the chronology of his ordination are recorded unevenly, and his journals were edited by friends and by himself.

literary_identity: Congregational minister and the principal teacher of his generation of Dissenting pastors, whose Family Expositor and Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul joined practical divinity to a wide philosophical charity.
biography: Born in London in 1702, the youngest of twenty children, of whom only he and one sister reached adulthood, he was briefly apprenticed, then educated largely by his own reading with the help of neighbouring ministers, and began to preach as a teenager. He held a country charge at Kibworth Harborough and settled at Northampton, where he led a large congregation and kept the academy that educated many Dissenting ministers of the following generation. His writings were at once devotional, instructional and practical: the Family Expositor, a commentary for household reading issued in parts from 1739, the Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul (1745), sermons, letters and a psalmody, with posthumous collections of his lectures and hymns. His courtesy, his stress on the inward work of grace and his readiness to commend experimental religion across party lines made him the best-loved of the Dissenting divines; his works were read by Edwards and by the American revivalists, and his academy trained preachers for England and the colonies. A failing chest sent him south for the winter of 1750, and he died at Lisbon in October 1751.
literary_profile: A pastoral writer of method and tenderness who brought the academy, the family desk and the congregation into one plan of religious education.
stylistic_characteristics: Warm, lucid, closely organised prose; commentary arranged for reading aloud in the family; case-divinity addressed to the conscience; a temperate ecumenical charity of phrase.
intellectual_concerns: The conduct and progress of religion in the soul; scripture read with the help of the learned and the critical; Dissenting education and the qualifications of the ministry; the duties of family worship; the friendship of Christians across parties.
historical_significance: He gave English Nonconformity its most influential programme of piety and ministerial training, and his books on the inner history of conversion shaped evangelical spirituality in Britain and America.
biographical_uncertainty: Several of his works were assembled and edited after his death from sermons and lectures, so their dates and completeness are uncertain.

literary_identity: Independent minister, logician and the father of English hymnody, who taught Dissent to sing its own composed songs and wrote a textbook of reasoning used on both sides of the Atlantic.
biography: Born at Southampton in 1674, the eldest of the children of a Southampton Nonconformist family whose father suffered imprisonment for religious meetings, he showed a remarkable gift for Latin as a child and was educated for the ministry under Dissenting tutors. He preached early and reluctantly, held a small charge in the country, and settled in London, where from the early 1690s he led the Independent assembly in Mark Lane and built one of the largest and most cultivated congregations in Dissent. His hymns and songs of worship began with the Horae Lyricae and the Hymns and Spiritual Songs of 1707, followed by Divine and Moral Songs for Children and by his bold paraphrases of the psalms, which provoked long disputes about whether congregations might sing anything not taken from the biblical psalter. His Logic, or the Art of Reasoning, his Improvement of the Mind and his theological and homiletic works made him a standard author for schools and preachers. Suspected by some of abandoning the Trinity, he was honoured with a doctorate and spent his last decades an invalid, still writing and visiting, until his death in November 1748; he was buried at Bunhill Fields.
literary_profile: The scholar-preacher of hymns and rules of thinking, who joined catechetical plainness to a lyricist's sense of meter and of congregational feeling.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, taught, unhurried prose in his logic and divinity; hymn verse in simple common measures with strong doctrinal structure and affective immediacy; a psalm paraphrase of dignified warmth.
intellectual_concerns: The signs, ideas and method of right reasoning; human composition in worship and the education of a singing people; the doctrine of the atonement and the disputed Trinity; childhood, catechism and the piety of the common Christian.
historical_significance: He invented the English congregation hymn and made it the vehicle of doctrine, and his Logic was a chief instrument of education for a century, used by Dissenters, Anglicans and the American colleges alike.
major_influences: the Bible and the Latin psalters
the Nonconformist ministry of his father's party
biographical_uncertainty: The precise sequence of his early pastoral settlements is uncertain, and the authorship of a few works printed under his name has been debated.

literary_identity: Former slave-ship captain turned Anglican minister and hymn-writer, whose Authentic Narrative (1764) and Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788) made a converted trader the most searched witness against the trade.
biography: Born in London in 1725, the son of a sea captain, and left largely to his own devices after the early death of his mother in his seventh year, he ran to sea as a lad, was pressed into the navy, flogged for desertion and then carried on the slave ships between West Africa and the Americas, where for a time he was in effect the property of an African owner. A violent storm in 1748 opened a religious conversion that he never forgot, although he continued in the trade and rose to be the master of a slave ship before illness and conscience ended his sea service in the mid-1750s. He left the sea in the mid-1750s, held a minor shore appointment, married and studied for the ministry, and published in 1764 An Authentic Narrative, an account of his mercy and of his former occupation that was widely read. About the same time he was appointed curate of Olney in Buckinghamshire, where he became the friend and guide of William Cowper and gave the village its hymn book of 1779. Presented in 1780 to St Mary Woolnoth in the City of London, he preached there for the rest of his life, consulted the parliamentary abolitionists and gave them Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788), a belated and unsparing self-accusation. He died in London in December 1807, having written the inscription for his own grave.
literary_profile: A pastor of the converted sinner who wrote his own career as a case of grace and then pressed that case into public argument against the trade that had made him.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, nautical and self-examining narrative prose; homely, concrete hymn verse in familiar metres; sermons built of plain doctrine pressed home; a letter-writer's intimacy and candour.
intellectual_concerns: Grace, remorse and the reality of change; the guilt of the slave trade and the complicity of churches and nations; providence in the lives of sailors; assurance, obedience and comfort for the afflicted.
historical_significance: His narrative and his 1788 tract supplied the abolitionist movement with its most credible first-hand testimony, and his hymns, written with Cowper, remain part of the ordinary worship of English-speaking Christianity.
major_influences: the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer
Thomas Scott and the Olney circle
biographical_uncertainty: His early years and the details of his service in Africa are known chiefly from his own narrative, which shapes the facts to a providential design.

literary_identity: Country clergyman and devotional writer, the most ornate of the meditative prose writers between Browne and the lake poets, author of Meditations among the Tombs (1746) and Theron and Aspasio (1755).
biography: Born at Hardingstone in Northamptonshire in 1714 into a family of small means and many children, he was educated for the church at Oxford, where he sat at Lincoln College, and took holy orders. Delicate and retired by temperament, he served country parishes, chiefly in Suffolk, under the patronage of great neighbours, and passed his short life among books, correspondence and the composition of devotional essays. His Meditations among the Tombs (1746) made at once a new fashion for the graveyard reverie and a reputation for splendid, melancholy prose; other volumes of meditations, letters and dialogues followed, together with a psalmody and hymns. Theron and Aspasio (1755), a long set of dialogues on natural and revealed religion, was read by its author as a defence of scriptural Christianity against deism and by John Wesley as a masked enthusiasm, and the attack pursued him for the rest of his days. He died suddenly at the end of 1758, still in his forties, and his works were repeatedly reprinted and translated.
literary_profile: A rhetorician of devotion, who turned the cemetery, the grove and the fireside into stages for the meditation on death, providence and the soul.
stylistic_characteristics: Richly ornamented, Latinate periodic prose; personification and apostrophe pressed to the edge of excess; dialogue and epistolary forms; a colour sense of leaves, twilight and marble that the next century would inherit.
intellectual_concerns: Death, immortality and the resurrection of the body; the evidences and the inward experience of revealed religion; the piety of natural scenery; taste, ornament and the uses of melancholy.
historical_significance: He fixed the graveyard meditation as a literary mode and supplied the ornate devotional prose that Johnson, the romantic naturists and the nineteenth-century tractarians all read; his controversy with Wesley sharpened the century's quarrel about enthusiasm and conversion.
major_influences: the Psalms and the Book of Common Prayer
biographical_uncertainty: The details of his preferments and patronage are slight, and the chronology of his several volumes is confused by reissues and collected editions.

literary_identity: Selborne naturalist and clergyman whose Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne (1789), assembled from letters to correspondents, founded the English observation of the living world.
biography: Born at Selborne in 1720 into a family of Hampshire clergymen and college men, he was educated at Winchester and at Oriel College, Oxford, took holy orders, and returned to the parish of his birth, of which he held the living. He never married and spent his income on his books and collections. For decades he kept registers of the weather and of the dates of flowering, bird arrival, nesting and hibernation, and he tested his questions by experiment, on the torpor of tortoises and bats, on the flight of swifts and swallows, on the insect world and on the habits of the field and the garden. His letters on these matters went to the Royal Society and to correspondents, above all to Daines Barrington and to the naturalist Thomas Pennant, whose questions and his own made the printed book. His book appeared at last in 1789, cast as a correspondence, and its two parts were quickly followed by a third volume of further letters. He died at Selborne in 1793.
literary_profile: The quiet observer of a single parish, whose method of numbered dates, experiment and plain statement made small facts carry weight.
stylistic_characteristics: Epistolary, unhurried and exact prose; dated field entries and the language of experiment; a naturalist's precision joined to a countryman's affection and gentle humour.
intellectual_concerns: The seasonal movements and instincts of birds and beasts; the limits of the systems of the schools; local history, antiquities and the surface of an English parish; the evidence of patient observation against the authority of books.
historical_significance: His book became the most beloved of English natural histories and a model for field biology, phenology and the whole later literature of the countryside.
major_influences: the parish registers of his father's church
biographical_uncertainty: The dating of his observations and the relation between the manuscript journals and the printed letters have been re-examined by later editors.

literary_identity: Physician, inventor and didactic poet of the Midlands Enlightenment, who put Linnaean botany, the chemistry of the senses and the transmutation of organs into heroic verse.
biography: Born at Elston in Nottinghamshire in 1731, the seventh child of a small landowner, he was educated at a school in the neighbouring town and at St John's College, Cambridge, where he won a reputation as a Latin poet, and completed his medical training in the north. He settled as a physician at Nottingham and then at Derby from the mid-1750s, and built one of the widest provincial practices in England, visiting patients over the counties about him. At Derby he became the friend and neighbour of the manufacturers, potters and natural philosophers who met in the Lunar Society, helped to found the Derby Philosophical Society in 1783, and occupied himself with canals, drainage and agricultural machinery. His poems made the new science readable: the first published part of his projected Botanic Garden, The Loves of the Plants, appeared in 1789 with elaborate prose notes, and its companion The Economy of Vegetation followed in 1791. His prose speculations on life, Zoonomia (volume one in 1794), and the poem The Temple of Nature (1803), belong to the years after the period covered here; both scandalised the pious and anticipated debates about the derivation of species. He died at Derby in April 1802, the grandfather of Charles Darwin.
literary_profile: The poet of the senses and of machinery, who wrote physiology, botany and agriculture as a single animated system of pleasure and use.
stylistic_characteristics: Couplet didactic verse of florid energy, with personified plants, sexual metaphor and an appeal to the five senses; long explanatory prose notes; exuberant, sometimes overreaching imagery.
intellectual_concerns: The Linnaean sexual system and the culture of plants; the chemistry of sensation, irritation and the motions of living bodies; the improvement of agriculture, machinery and public health; the derivation and progress of organic life; the rights of reason against priestcraft.
historical_significance: He carried the scientific Enlightenment into English verse and into provincial industry, and his speculations on life made him one of the ancestors of evolutionary biology as well as the grandfather of its founder.
major_influences: David Hartley and the associationist physiology
biographical_uncertainty: His early education and medical qualifications are imperfectly recorded, and the chronology of the parts of the Botanic Garden is complicated by pirated and revised printings.

birthplace: Essaka, in the interior of what is now Nigeria (contested; a birth in South Carolina has also been argued)
nationality_or_literary_tradition: British abolitionist writing of the African diaspora
literary_identity: Formerly enslaved mariner and author of The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African (1789), the founding text of the English-speaking slave narrative and of abolitionist argument.
biography: Born about 1745, he recorded his childhood in the village of Essaka, in the interior of what is now southern Nigeria; the archival work of Vincent Carretta has raised the alternative that he was born in South Carolina, and the question is still debated. Brought into the trade as a child and carried to the West Indies, he was purchased by a naval officer, taken to England, christened and given the name by which he published, and afterwards served at sea in North America and the West Indies. In 1766 he bought his own freedom, worked as a mariner and merchant, went north with an Arctic voyage in 1773, settling in London, where he joined Methodist and abolitionist circles and made a living by his pen and his lectures. His Interesting Narrative appeared in 1789 by subscription, ran into several editions in his lifetime and was translated into several languages, and it became the standard account of the horrors of the middle passage. In 1791, after the period covered here, he was appointed to office in the Sierra Leone enterprise; he married an Englishwoman in 1792 and had children. He died in London in March 1797.
literary_profile: An autobiographer who combined the captive's narrative, the Methodist conversion account and the commercial self-assessment to make a claim on the reader's reason and pity.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, orderly, controlled first-person narrative; catalogues of ship, cargo, price and place used as evidence; horror reported without rant; a scriptural and civic vocabulary of liberty, brotherhood and redress.
