intellectual_concerns: The evil and the economics of the slave trade; the capacity and the humanity of Africans; the religion of the converted captive; the rights of British subjects regardless of colour; the moral danger of colonial luxury to the metropole.
historical_significance: His Narrative was a decisive instrument of the abolitionist campaign and the earliest and most influential of the Atlantic slave narratives, still read as a foundation text of African-diaspora writing.
major_influences: Granville Sharp and the London abolitionists
the tradition of captivity and travel narratives
the writings of the Quaker and Anglican opponents of the trade
biographical_uncertainty: His birthplace, date of birth and the details of his early captivity remain contested, since the archival record does not confirm the account he printed of himself.

birthplace: the Gold Coast (the Fante coastal region of present-day Ghana; the town is given variously)
nationality_or_literary_tradition: British abolitionist writing of the African diaspora
literary_identity: Formerly enslaved writer and campaigner in London, author of Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species (1787), the century's most radical English abolitionist argument.
biography: Born on the Gold Coast in the 1750s, he was kidnapped as a child, sold among the coastal forts and carried to Grenada, from which he was brought to England in the early 1770s. Named John Stuart in service, he remained in England a free man and joined the small circle of free Black Londoners clustered about Granville Sharp, for whom he acted as an intermediary and whose legal cases he helped to press. His Thoughts and Sentiments, published in 1787 and reprinted in the following years, argued from natural rights, scripture and the law of nations that the trade and slaveholding were crimes requiring restitution, and it demanded an end to the commerce rather than amelioration of it. He addressed the British public, the legislature and the slaveholders directly, and urged the commercial and religious advantages of an intercourse with Africa. He witnessed and advised in the campaigns of the later 1780s, and a shortened version of his book appeared in 1791. Nothing certain is known of him afterwards; he is usually supposed to have died about 1791.
literary_profile: A philosopher of natural rights from inside the experience of enslavement, who reasoned from first principles to restitution and to the equality of all mankind.
stylistic_characteristics: Earnest, tightly argued prose of principle; scriptural and legal citation pressed into a single moral case; direct address to monarchs, merchants and slaves; a dignity that refuses apology.
intellectual_concerns: Natural liberty and the sin of man-stealing; the rights of Africans and the duties of Britain; restitution and compensation; the abolition of the trade rather than the reform of slavery; the religious and commercial future of Africa.
historical_significance: He supplied the abolitionist movement with its most uncompromising theoretical case and the first English book by a formerly enslaved writer to argue for total abolition, and his work stands beside Equiano's as a founding document of African-diaspora writing.
major_influences: Olaudah Equiano and the London abolitionists
the natural-rights and scripture traditions of Protestant argument
the Quaker and Methodist protests against the trade
biographical_uncertainty: His year of birth is approximate, the town of his birth is variously reported, and the date of his death is unknown; no record of him is certainly identified after 1791.

literary_identity: London merchant's apprentice turned jurist-divine, the first great legal strategist of British abolition, who made the condition of enslaved people in England a question of common law.
biography: Born at Durham in 1735 into a large clerical family, he was apprenticed to a London draper at fifteen and, with the help of a legacy, kept himself free for study, mastering law, divinity, biblical languages, music and a remarkable range of authors. A beaten black servant, Jonathan Strong, whom his brother's hospital had discharged, drew him in the mid-1760s into the question of whether a man could be held as property in England, and he answered it by research and by litigation. He gave counsel and money to the test cases of the following years, and the cause of James Somerset, argued before Lord Mansfield in 1772, was pressed forward by his advice and reporting. He printed legal essays and letters maintaining that slavery had no footing in English law, corresponded with governors and colonists, promoted schemes for settling freed people in Africa, and was among the founders of the committee of 1787 for the abolition of the trade, in which Ottobah Cugoano lived and worked in his household. He wrote also on prophecy, on translation and on the affairs of the church, and died unmarried at Fulham on 6 July 1813, buried in the churchyard there.
literary_profile: A lay lawyer of immense industry who read texts, digested opinions and turned scholarship into an instrument for the deliverance of individuals.
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, citational and dogged prose; folio-long footnotes of law, scripture and the fathers; argument built from authority pressed to a single conclusion; a devout and combative directness.
intellectual_concerns: The legal status of persons on English soil; the sin and the policy of the slave trade; the rights of the individual against magistrates and merchants; the interpretation of prophecy and of the languages of the Bible; the duty of public charity.
historical_significance: He made the Somerset judgment possible and founded the legal and organisational base of British abolition, standing beside Wilberforce and Equiano as an architect of the movement that ended the trade.
major_influences: the Bible and his family's clerical learning
the common-law and civil-law reading he pursued alone
the Quaker and colonial protests against slavery
biographical_uncertainty: The exact contribution of his advisers and of Cugoano to his papers and cases is difficult to separate, and his chronology of the earlier suits is debated.

literary_identity: Naval surgeon and West India clergyman whose Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves (1784) supplied the abolitionist movement with its documentation and its moral case.
biography: Born at Fraserburgh in Aberdeenshire in 1733 and educated for medicine, he served as a surgeon in the navy, was present in the West Indies, and after leaving the service settled as a planter's physician and then as a clergyman on the sugar islands, where he saw the working of the slave system at its worst and quarrelled with the island planters over it. Ordained and returned to England, he was given the living of Teston in Kent, where the Bouverie family became his friends and encouragement, and there he wrote his Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies (1784). Its companion volume, an Inquiry into the effects of stopping the African trade and opening a commerce with Africa, argued that emancipation and lawful trade would enrich the nation. The sugar interest answered him in a swarm of hostile pamphlets, attacked his conduct as a planter and as a clergyman, and pursued him over his account of the killing of mutinous ratings on a king's ship; he replied at length and lost certain friends by his stubbornness. He advised the committee formed in 1787 and instructed its members in the evidence of the colonies. He died in 1789, the year of Equiano's narrative, leaving the Teston circle to carry his arguments into Parliament.
literary_profile: The witness-clergyman, who made an accumulated case of particulars, dates and amounts out of twenty years of service in the slave-holding islands.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, accumulative, heavily evidenced prose; narrative of cases joined to statistical and scriptural argument; a surgeon's specification of wounds and punishments; occasional bitterness of reply.
intellectual_concerns: The treatment, conversion and education of enslaved people; the criminality of the trade and the duty of the nation; the economics of emancipation and of African commerce; the moral responsibility of the planter and the clergy.
historical_significance: His two books of 1784 converted a clerical protest into the printed evidence on which the organised abolition campaign of the following decade was built, and the circle he gathered at Teston became a nursery of the Clapham reformers.
major_influences: his naval and West India experience
the evangelical revival and the religious societies
the Quaker protest against the trade
biographical_uncertainty: The dates of his island ministry and of his ordination are reported inconsistently, and the details of the controversy over the mutiny narrative are partisan on both sides.

literary_identity: Aberdeenshire-born physician of Queen Anne, mathematician and wit, the inventor of John Bull and the author of the design argument that later natural theology reused.
biography: Born at Marnoch in Aberdeenshire in 1667, the son of a Calvinist minister, he studied medicine at Aberdeen, took his degree in Scotland and removed to London, where he built a large and prosperous practice and was named one of the physicians to Queen Anne. He became the friend and adviser of Pope, Swift and Gay, and is held to have given the first impulse to the wits who met as the Scriblerus Club, while his own learned jokes about the arts and sciences supplied much of their matter. His essay on the usefulness of mathematical learning, published at the beginning of the century, put the argument from design in a form that was quoted for generations and that William Paley enlarged in his Natural Theology of 1802, long after the period covered here. In 1712 he wrote the History of John Bull, an allegory of the nation, its law and its trades, which gave English politics a permanent personification, and in the same year an essay on the art of political lying, an anatomy of party rhetoric. Pope addressed to him one of his most searching verses, and he died in London in February 1735.
literary_profile: A physician-mathematician who turned professional learning into political satire and moral argument, and whose allegory taught a nation to see itself as a character.
stylistic_characteristics: Dry, learned, deadpan irony; the allegorical case history and the law suit as national portrait; precise definitions and enumerations; a populariser's clarity about mathematics and medicine.
intellectual_concerns: The evidence of design in nature and the uses of mathematical reasoning; the mechanics of party, credit and national interest; the character of the English constitution and its trades; the corruption of political language; the mixture of learning and quackery in the arts.
historical_significance: He gave Augustan politics its national allegory and its analysis of spin, carried the design argument into ordinary English prose, and stood at the centre of the circle that produced the greatest satires of the age.
major_influences: the Scottish Calvinist divinity of his childhood
Isaac Newton and the new mathematics
the Royal Society tradition of medical and statistical enquiry
the Augustan pamphlet and party press
biographical_uncertainty: The ascription of individual pieces of Scriblerus work is unsettled, and the date of his London settlement and of his Scottish degree is variously reported.
